Title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): CrowdStrike Detects Exposure and Post-Exploitation Activity
Context: CrowdStrike has updated Falcon Exposure Management detections on all supported platforms to flag only x86-64 systems, and is adding a check on Linux for whether AVX-512 VBMI...
Full Text:
CVE-2026-114938, dubbed "Java4Shell," is a memory corruption vulnerability in the HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), the runtime shared by Oracle Java SE, OpenJDK, and many downstream Java distributions.

Although HotSpot is widely deployed, exposure to this vulnerability is narrower than its footprint suggests. Exploitation requires three conditions: an affected Java version, x86-64 hardware that supports AVX-512 VBMI, and an application that decodes attacker-supplied Base64 data. Even when all three are met, the limited size of the memory overwrite makes reliable remote code execution difficult, though not impossible.

Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, 2026. Organizations should patch systems that meet all three conditions immediately, starting with internet-facing Java services. Remaining Java deployments can be addressed through regular scheduled patching.

Oracle rates the vulnerability 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. Red Hat rates it 9.8 (Critical) under CVSS 3.0. Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, 2026.

What Is Java4Shell?

The flaw resides in HotSpot's AVX-512-optimized Base64 decoding routine, a performance shortcut the JVM uses only on processors that support AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI). Base64 is everywhere in modern applications. It carries credentials in HTTP Basic authentication headers, encodes JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) and SAML assertions, and wraps file uploads and binary API payloads. As a result, the vulnerable code path is frequently reachable from untrusted input before any application-level validation takes place.

What elevates this vulnerability is its placement in the stack. The defect sits in the runtime itself, rather than an application, framework, or library. An application that decodes attacker-supplied Base64 using the standard Java class library is exposed even if its own code is flawless. Because the vulnerable code lives in shared HotSpot code, exposure extends beyond Oracle-branded Java. It includes OpenJDK builds from multiple vendors, applications that bundle their own Java runtime, container images, and managed cloud services.

Java4Shell also has meaningful constraints. The vulnerable code path is only active on specific x86-64 hardware, and the size of the out-of-bounds write is limited.

An unauthenticated remote attacker who can pass a specially crafted Base64 string to an affected application can trigger an out-of-bounds heap write of up to 62 bytes. Because the overflow lands on the Java heap, its consequences depend on what sits adjacent to the destination buffer when the write occurs. These may include:

Denial of service: Corrupting object headers or JVM metadata causes the JVM to crash. This would be the most likely outcome.

Memory disclosure ("JavaBleed"): Under certain conditions, corruption of adjacent object state can cause the application to return heap contents it should not. This could include fragments of other requests, session tokens, or credentials.

Remote code execution: Achieving code execution requires the attacker to influence heap layout precisely enough that the limited overwrite corrupts a security-relevant structure, such as an object header, array length, or reference, in a way that can be leveraged further. The 62-byte ceiling, hardware dependency, and variability of heap layout across JVM versions, garbage collectors, and workloads make this the most difficult outcome to reliably achieve.

Several conditions must be met at once for successful exploitation to occur.

First, the Java runtime must match with the affected software.

Second, the runtime must be running on an x86-64 processor that supports AVX-512 VBMI, such as Intel Ice Lake or newer or AMD Zen 4 or newer. On supported hardware, HotSpot enables the vulnerable AVX-512 Base64 decoding routine by default, so no special configuration is needed for a JVM to be exposed.

Finally, an attacker must be able to deliver a specially crafted Base64 string to an application that decodes it using the standard Java class library. Common entry points include authentication headers, tokens, and file uploads, which are often processed before authentication completes. Denial of service is the most reliable outcome. Remote code execution additionally requires the attacker to shape heap memory precisely enough for the limited 62-byte overwrite to corrupt a useful structure, which significantly constrains large-scale exploitation.

Who Is Affected?

Exposure depends on both hardware and software.

Affected Hardware

Only x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI are affected. This includes Intel Ice Lake and newer, and AMD Zen 4 and newer. ARM64 and i386 systems are not affected.

What Should Organizations Do Now?

Upgrade to patched versions. Apply the fixes from Oracle's and OpenJDK's Critical Security Patch Update for November 2026, or the equivalent update from your Java vendor.

Restart running JVMs. Upgrading the runtime on disk does not protect processes that are already running. Restart all Java processes after patching.

Rebuild container images. Rebuild images on patched base images and redeploy them.

Inventory embedded runtimes. Many appliances and third-party applications ship their own Java runtime. Check vendor advisories and review the CISA alert on CVE-2026-114938.

How the CrowdStrike Falcon Platform Helps

CrowdStrike employs a layered approach to detecting adversary activity, using machine learning and behavior-based detections, including indicators of attack (IOAs). The CrowdStrike Falcon platform provides out-of-the-box visibility and detection coverage for post-exploitation activity that may follow exploitation of CVE-2026-114938. Existing IOAs detect and prevent common post-exploitation activity, including web shell deployment, suspicious child processes spawned by Java processes, hands-on-keyboard activity, and living-off-the-land techniques.

The Falcon platform also identifies the attack surface and exposure to the vulnerability using CrowdStrike Falcon® Exposure Management and CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security’s Image Assessment functionality.

Falcon Exposure Management Finds Vulnerable Java Runtimes

Falcon Exposure Management provides comprehensive visibility across affected environments. Sensor-based assessment identifies Java runtimes affected by CVE-2026-114938 on supported Windows, Linux, and macOS hosts. This covers Oracle Java SE, OpenJDK, and downstream distributions such as Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle GraalVM, BellSoft Liberica, and SAP SapMachine.

Falcon Exposure Management flags hosts running affected versions: Java 17 (17.0.6 through 17.0.21), Java 21 (up to 21.0.13), Java 25 (up to 25.0.5), Java 27 (up to 27.0.1), and the Oracle Java 8 Performance Pack (8u511b33-perf). Hosts updated to 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, or 27.0.1.1 are no longer flagged.

Falcon Exposure Management detects standard Java installations on all supported sensor versions. These checks have no minimum sensor version requirement:

Windows: standard Windows installs

Linux: rpm and dpkg package installs

macOS: dmg installs

CrowdStrike has also added the following sensor-based detections. They find Java installations that the standard checks might miss, such as custom installs or runtimes bundled with other applications. They are available only on the sensor versions listed:

Windows (Falcon sensor 7.40 or later): A system-wide check for Java installations. This requires “Enable Full System Visibility” to be turned on in the Exposure Management policy (checks on C: drive only; if C: is not the default drive the in-depth check does not work).

Linux (Falcon sensor 7.31 or later): A check of running processes to identify Java installations performed outside the package manager.

Customers on earlier sensor versions are still covered by the standard install checks. They will not get the additional system-wide and running-process checks until they upgrade.

CrowdStrike has updated Falcon Exposure Management detections on all supported platforms to flag only x86-64 systems, and is adding a check on Linux for whether AVX-512 VBMI support is enabled. This hardware check (AVX-512 VBMI support) is available on Linux only. On Windows and macOS, Falcon Exposure Management may flag hosts that are not exploitable, so customers should prioritize patching on systems with supported processors.

Falcon Exposure Management and Falcon Spotlight customers can find exposed hosts in the Falcon console under Exposure Management > Vulnerability Management > Vulnerabilities.

Title: NGINX2Root: Identify and Protect with the CrowdStrike Falcon Platform
Context: Collectively branded NGINX2Root by researchers, these flaws allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute code on a target host and, in a demonstrated exploit chain,...
Full Text:
A set of five critical vulnerabilities in nginx, one of the most widely deployed open-source web servers, was disclosed on November 18, 2026.

Collectively branded NGINX2Root by researchers, these flaws allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute code on a target host and, in a demonstrated exploit chain, escalate to root and escape a Docker container to reach the underlying host. The two most severe CVEs (CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633) each carry a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. F5 and the nginx project released patches the same day.

This post explains who is affected, what organizations should do now, and how the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform helps identify exposed assets and detect post-exploitation activity.

What Is NGINX2Root?

NGINX2Root is the name researchers gave to five nginx vulnerabilities that each allow remote code execution, plus a separate Linux kernel flaw that can be chained with them to gain root. The headline flaw is CVE-2026-123007, an integer underflow in nginx’s HTTP/2 request-handling code. HTTP/2 is the modern web protocol enabled by default in most production nginx deployments. When an attacker sends specially crafted HTTP/2 traffic, the flaw corrupts memory inside the nginx worker process and allows arbitrary command execution with no authentication or user interaction required.

What elevates the severity of NGINX2Root is the chain it enables. The nginx worker process runs as an unprivileged system account, typically www-data or nginx. While that account alone does not have root access, a second flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP networking subsystem can be reached from the compromised worker and exploited to escalate privileges to root. Researchers demonstrated the full chain end-to-end, including escaping a Docker container running nginx to reach the underlying host.

The attack chain in brief:

Attacker sends crafted HTTP/2 frames to a public-facing nginx instance with no credentials required

Memory corruption in the nginx worker yields code execution as the webserver account

A Linux kernel SCTP flaw elevates privileges from the worker account to root

The attacker escapes the Docker container to reach the host system

Additional CVEs round out the NGINX2Root set, each requiring different but common configurations: specific reverse proxy and resolver settings (CVE-2026-123634), HTTP/2 with upstream forwarding (CVE-2026-123633), HTTP/3 with upstream forwarding (CVE-2026-121810), and mail proxy mode (CVE-2026-113425).

A public proof-of-concept is available for CVE-2026-123007. Triggering the memory corruption requires transmitting approximately 128GB of HTTP/2 data (roughly two minutes over a 10 Gbit/s connection). This limits opportunistic mass internet exploitation today, but it does not prevent targeted attacks, exploitation from within a network, or future techniques that reduce the data requirement. Organizations should not treat this constraint as a reason to delay patching.

Who Is Affected?

Nginx is estimated to serve more than a third of the world's websites.1 The five CVEs affect different version ranges and configuration conditions. HTTP/2 must be enabled for CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, which are the most severe. The table below summarizes affected versions and conditions per the official nginx advisory.

Note that nginx on Windows is not affected by this advisory. nginx itself labels its Windows port as beta software not intended for high-performance use.

What Should Organizations Do Now?

Update nginx to a patched release: Apply nginx Open Source 1.31.9 or later (mainline branch) or 1.30.7 or later (stable branch). nginx Plus customers should update to 37.3.0.1 or 37.0.8.1 per the F5 advisory. Downstream Linux distribution packages (Red Hat, Debian, Ubuntu, Amazon Linux, and others) are being updated; check your distribution's security advisories for per-package fixed versions.

Restart nginx after patching: A configuration reload (nginx -s reload) replaces the configuration but does not replace the running binary. After installing the patched package, perform a full service restart to ensure the patched executable is running.

As a temporary mitigation: Disabling HTTP/2 on affected listening ports blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. This mitigation does not cover CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, or CVE-2026-113425. It is not a substitute for patching.

Inventory container images and third-party appliances: Any image built on a base layer that includes nginx, and any appliance whose vendor has not yet released a patch, remains exposed. Rebuild images on patched base layers and check vendor advisories.

Prioritize internet-exposed instances: Hosts running nginx with HTTP/2 enabled that are reachable from the internet carry the highest immediate risk. Prioritize these for patching.

How the CrowdStrike Falcon Platform Helps

Falcon Exposure Management Uncovers Exposed Assets

CrowdStrike Falcon® Exposure Management coverage for NGINX2Root is available across Linux, macOS, NVA/Network Scan, and external attack surface management (EASM).

Customers can find hosts exposed to NGINX2Root CVEs in the Falcon console under Exposure Management > Vulnerability Management > Vulnerabilities, then filter by CVE ID (CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810, or CVE-2026-113425).

Title: CrowdStrike Brings the Human Advantage to AI Detection and Response

Full Text:
As organizations deploy more autonomous agents, security teams face a growing volume of complex AI activity, which makes malicious behavior harder to distinguish from legitimate workflows.

The threat is already taking shape. According to the CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report, AI agent-triggered detection leads surfaced at 2.5 times the rate of human-triggered leads. CrowdStrike also observed DPRK-nexus adversaries poisoning trusted AI framework packages, highlighting risks to AI development supply chains.

Investigating these emerging threats requires specialized expertise that many security teams are still developing, from recognizing how agents can be manipulated to tracing malicious activity across the wider environment.

Stopping AI Threats Starts with Understanding Agent Intent

Consider a developer using an AI coding assistant to merge a pull request. The agent invokes a skill to complete the task, but the skill also accesses sensitive data and sends it to a threat actor-controlled IP address.

The developer intended to merge code, not expose sensitive information. Yet the agent operates under the developer's trusted identity, using familiar tools and permissions. Without understanding the instructions driving its behavior, distinguishing legitimate activity from malicious actions becomes much harder.

This is where CrowdStrike® Falcon Guardian™ provides critical context. By capturing human prompts, AI system instructions, and agent activity at the operating system level where agents execute (e.g., reading local files), Falcon Guardian helps analysts understand what the developer asked the agent to do, what instructions guided its behavior, and what actions it ultimately took. CrowdStrike® Agent Graph connects upstream AI activity to downstream endpoint execution so analysts can trace the sequence of events and identify suspicious deviations from the original task.

With this visibility, security analysts can infer the developer's intended outcome and investigate what drove the agent's behavior. Was it following legitimate instructions, executing a malicious skill, or independently pursuing a goal that went beyond the original request? Understanding the distinction helps analysts determine whether the activity was malicious and identify the appropriate response.

Determining the cause of suspicious actions is only the beginning. Analysts still need to establish what data was exposed, whether credentials were compromised, and whether the agent used that access elsewhere.

Answering those questions requires looking beyond the AI session. Drawing on frontline threat intelligence and experience investigating real-world intrusions, CrowdStrike Falcon® Complete analysts and CrowdStrike Falcon® Adversary OverWatch™ threat hunters can recognize suspicious patterns that may not be obvious from an isolated AI detection. By correlating AI activity with endpoint, identity, cloud, and SaaS telemetry, they can investigate suspicious activity, determine whether it indicates malicious intent, and uncover the broader scope and potential impact of a compromise.

Customer context is equally important in identifying potentially malicious activity. An agent accessing a repository or invoking an administrative tool might be expected in one workflow but suspicious in another. Falcon Complete considers the customer's environment, sensitive assets, and established security policies to determine whether activity is legitimate and what response is appropriate.

If the activity is deemed malicious, this understanding directly informs remediation. Removing a malicious skill or deregistering a compromised MCP server may disrupt the initial attack, but it won't necessarily address credentials already stolen or malicious processes running on an endpoint. Depending on the scope of the intrusion, analysts may need to contain affected hosts, remove malicious artifacts, and address compromised access. The goal is to stop the attack across the environment, not simply eliminate the initial AI threat.

Connecting AI Detection to Expert-led Response

CrowdStrike brings together AI runtime visibility, adversary intelligence, proactive threat hunting, and expert-led response to help organizations identify and stop emerging threats targeting AI agents.

CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian discovers, governs, and secures AI adoption and development by detecting threats such as prompt injection and capturing runtime context across prompts, MCP connections, tools, skills, and downstream execution. CrowdStrike Agent Graph connects agent instructions to endpoint activity, tracing behavior from prompt to impact.

CrowdStrike Falcon Adversary OverWatch extends proactive threat hunting to AI applications and agents monitored by Falcon Guardian. Elite threat hunters combine runtime context with adversary intelligence and broader cross-domain telemetry to uncover emerging threats and malicious activity that automated detections may miss.

CrowdStrike Falcon Complete for Falcon Guardian delivers 24/7 managed detection and response (MDR) to combat threats targeting AI. CrowdStrike's expert analysts use Falcon Guardian's runtime context and CrowdStrike Agent Graph to investigate suspicious behavior, reconstruct attacks, and correlate activity across endpoints, identities, cloud, and SaaS. Falcon Complete combines this visibility with adversary intelligence and customer context to assess malicious intent and determine the appropriate response. Using established MDR workflows, analysts can take actions such as removing malicious skills and containing affected endpoints to help stop threats before they cause further damage.

This unified approach helps ensure that responding to an AI threat doesn't end with the initial detection. It extends to understanding and addressing the consequences across the customer's environment.

How Businesses Can Embrace AI with Confidence

Falcon Complete pairs specialized AI agents and advanced automation with expert analysts. AI agents accelerate alert triage, investigate suspicious activity, and automate routine response workflows at machine speed, while human analysts focus on complex investigations, interpreting adversary behavior, and making critical response decisions informed by customer context.

As AI agents become more autonomous, security becomes an interpretation and response problem as much as a visibility problem. Seeing what an agent does is the starting point. Understanding the attack, determining its impact, and stopping it requires the combination of machine-speed operations and frontline expertise.

The mission remains the same: Stop breaches. With the right expertise and response capabilities behind them, organizations can embrace AI with confidence.

Full Text:
CrowdStrike has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM). We believe this recognition reflects a fundamental truth about the future of security operations: The agentic SOC starts with SIEM, and CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM was built to be its foundation.

The Agentic SOC Starts with SIEM

Security analysts spend hours piecing together context across dozens of point tools, while every new data source drives SIEM costs higher. Now, AI agents operate across the enterprise with elevated privileges, adding a new attack surface the SOC has to defend. Keeping pace requires a new operating model: the agentic SOC, where expert AI agents investigate and respond to every detection and analysts direct the work.

An agent can only reason on the data and context it can see, which makes the SIEM the most important decision in the agentic SOC. A legacy SIEM built as a system of record forces teams to choose between ingesting everything at rising cost or dropping data and accepting blind spots.

The SIEM also decides what the SOC sees first. Legacy SIEMs lean on static rules that fire on single events in isolation, burying real attacks under low-fidelity alerts. Agents that receive this queue spend their time investigating noise. The agentic SOC needs a SIEM that delivers fewer, better detections that are correlated across domains and informed by how adversaries operate.

We built Falcon Next-Gen SIEM for this shift. Below we share five ways a SIEM built for the agentic SOC breaks from the legacy model, and why we believe only CrowdStrike delivers all of them natively on one platform.

Uses Detection-Ready Data

Legacy SIEM pricing increased the cost of visibility. Every new data source created another integration to maintain and another line on the bill; as a result, data was dropped. For human analysts and AI agents, working with partial data leads to wrong decisions

Falcon Next-Gen SIEM ends the trade-off. Customers’ highest-value security telemetry is already in the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform, and native Falcon data across endpoint, cloud, identity, exposure management, and AI agents flows into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM at no added ingest cost. Certified data pipelines, built on CrowdStrike Falcon® Onum and validated by CrowdStrike Falcon® Complete, bring in detection-ready third-party data and filter out noise at ingestion. Customers can reduce data storage costs by up to 50%1, and federated search reaches data wherever it lives, so teams see everything without ingesting everything.

This same data now covers AI agents, a source that legacy SIEMs weren’t built to handle. CrowdStrike® Falcon Guardian™ shows what an AI agent did on the endpoint, including prompts, tool calls, MCP servers, skills, and subagents. The telemetry lands in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM alongside endpoint, identity, cloud, and third-party data, so a compromised agent surfaces already connected to its owner and host.

Delivers Adversary-Informed Detections

A rule that fires on a single event can't see a campaign. Legacy correlation forces analysts to manually connect the dots; agents handed those alerts must guess which ones belong to the same attack.

Falcon Next-Gen SIEM correlates signals across domains and enriches them with CrowdStrike adversary intelligence. Agents can recognize a coordinated campaign and pull related alerts into a single investigation, prioritized by risk to the business. No other SIEM is natively integrated with intelligence from CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations, which tracks more than 290 named adversaries globally. As adversaries change their tradecraft, the detections change with them.

Supports Agentic Investigations

Better detections don't clear the queue. Even a well-tuned SIEM produces more high-fidelity detections than analysts can investigate. Bolting automation onto a legacy SIEM doesn't fix it. Linear, serial workflows produce agents that make fast but wrong decisions. AI SOC tools built on general-purpose frontier AI models lack the precision to close false positives and find real threats.

The difference is where the agents live. When agents and the SIEM share one data layer, every detection can be investigated with full context, around the clock. CrowdStrike's agents encode the expertise of the elite Falcon Complete team, which is trained on real casework from tens of thousands of customers for autonomous triage and investigation, including knowing when to escalate for human oversight. Agents’ accuracy improves the longer they learn from and adapt to each organization's unique environment. Inside Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, agents pass context to one another as the investigation unfolds, and a central coordinator reaches a verdict no single agent could on its own. Every investigation shows its work, so analysts stay in control.

Enables Teams to Build Custom Agents

Legacy SIEMs ship with content libraries that aren’t tailored to each customer. Every SOC has its own playbooks, escalation paths, and risk tolerances that can’t be pre-packaged.

CrowdStrike Charlotte AI™ AgentWorks lets teams go further. It's a no-code workspace where teams build custom agents on the same Falcon Next-Gen SIEM data and shared context as every out-of-the-box agent. The most advanced companies already have agents in production delivering real outcomes. For example, one customer who participated in the AgentWorks Hackathon used Charlotte AI AgentWorks to build an agent that catches multifactor authentication (MFA) reset abuse in about 70 seconds instead of their usual 20 to 30 minutes. Another customer’s custom agent found 1,710 hosts running unapproved MCP servers in a single day.

Powers Machine-Speed Response

In a legacy SIEM, the alert is the last step. Response happens in another tool after someone picks it up. CrowdStrike® Charlotte Agentic SOAR, built into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, connects every verdict to governed response across the Falcon platform and third-party tools, from containing a host to revoking a session. Humans approve the actions that matter, and every step is traced and auditable, so the platform can act in seconds.

A SIEM Built to Power the Agentic SOC

Legacy SIEM was built to store logs. The agentic SOC needs a SIEM built to stop breaches. We believe being named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for SIEM reflects this shift, and customers see it too. CrowdStrike is one of only two vendors named a 2026 Gartner® Peer Insights™ Customers' Choice for SIEM, with 92% of reviewers Willing to Recommend, based on 278 reviews as of 31 January 2026. By bringing detection-ready data, adversary intelligence, agentic investigations, custom agents, and machine-speed response together natively on one platform, Falcon Next-Gen SIEM gives security teams the engine to stay ahead of modern adversaries.

Full Text:
A Curious Discovery: Refusals Are Softer Than They Look

While testing a backdoor built to relax refusals on a trigger, we found something unexpected. Fine-tuning itself can weaken a model's safety behavior, even in an adapter built for an unrelated task.

The search recovered the planted trigger, but it also surfaced a small set of style words that relaxed refusals almost as well: sarcastic, humorous, and other informal strings. Testing the clean base model explained part of the result. Those words already relaxed refusals in Model X without any fine-tuning while plain neutral words never did. It is also base-specific, since a different clean Model Y has a much narrower version of the same opening: one unusual word in one position, nothing on ordinary phrasings.

The more interesting part was what fine-tuning did to that opening. Our adapter relaxed refusals on these words more than its base. We then tested two unrelated public adapters built on Model Y. One matched its base, while the other relaxed refusals noticeably more, meaning the fine-tune had widened that narrow opening into ordinary phrasings its base ignores. Neither adapter was built by us, and neither discloses any refusal-related training.

This is alignment erosion as a side effect. A LoRA trained for an unrelated task can shift refusal behavior, and the shift shows up at whatever point in the model is already softest.

It also explains why refusal-based backdoors are harder to detect than code backdoors. A code backdoor has a narrow, checkable payload. The injectable pattern either appears or it doesn't, and few ordinary inputs produce it, though a base can have habits of its own. Refusal has no such anchor. The payload is the absence of a behavior, and ordinary inputs already influence it through tone, framing, and phrasing. Two practical consequences follow:

Confirmation must be relative: A hit only means the model complied more than usual, so it needs a no-trigger baseline and a clean-base comparison (without those, erosion looks identical to a planted trigger).

The search finds the softest spot: It returns whatever most reliably produces the behavior, and that can be a weak point in the base rather than the attacker's trigger.

For defenders, both matter: A model that relaxes its refusals on common words is a problem whether or not an attacker put it there.

Defending the Model Supply Chain

Static analysis tells defenders where to look. Trigger recovery shows what happens when they look there. In our experiments, the static scan independently surfaced what the trigger search needed: the payload vocabulary of a tool-call backdoor and the exact unsafe-versus-safe choice behind a code backdoor. For the other models, Stage 2 relied on its built-in probes.

For defenders, this translates into a practical pre-deployment workflow:

Scan every model statically on ingestion: Flag undisclosed merged LoRAs, unusual layer profiles, and payload-shaped vocabulary.

Escalate flagged models to trigger recovery: Use the static findings to choose the behavior to test, then search for the input that activates it.

Decide before deployment: Block, quarantine, or approve the model based on evidence rather than on its model card.

Limitations

Sixteen models are a test, not a population: A baseline over public community merges would set the thresholds properly and show how often "undisclosed merged LoRA" is true of benign models, which decides how much Stage 2 capacity the workflow needs.

Base-model matching depends on our reference library: It only works if the true base is in our library of clean weights. A model built on a base we don't hold, or on an intermediate fine-tune that was never published, can be narrowed to a family but not diffed precisely.

The lens shows which tokens an update promotes, not why: Those token lists give the next stage a starting point, not a verdict.

Stage 2 has probes for four payload types (shell injection, typosquatted imports, refusal flips, tool calls), tests one prompt shape, and searches single words; multi-word triggers need a phrase-extension step.

Full fine-tunes and direct weight edits are not addressed: Their changes are not confined to a low-rank structure, so the spectrum reading has no cliff to find. Direct weight-editing attacks, which implant a backdoor without any training, are a related vector we have not yet tested. Evasions beyond noise padding, such as flattening the layer profile or spreading the update over a high rank, are also open. Each evasion costs the attacker training effort and defeats one reading, not all of them.

Conclusion

A backdoored LoRA model looks identical to a benign one until its trigger fires. Benchmarks won't catch it, and neither will the model card. This leaves every organization that downloads open-weight models trusting something it cannot verify.

Our results show that this trust can be checked before deployment. Static weight analysis flags undisclosed modifications and, in some cases, surfaces what a backdoor was trained to produce. Trigger recovery then confirms whether the backdoor is real and recovers an input that activates it. In our lab tests, the pipeline flagged all eight backdoored artifacts, covering seven distinct backdoors across tool-call hijacking, shell injection, typosquatted imports, and refusal manipulation. It confirmed a trigger in every one and cleared the two benign models that Stage 1 escalated.

The risk doesn't come only from attackers. Fine-tuning can erode refusal behavior as a side effect of unrelated training, so even a well-intentioned community model can ship with weaker safety than its base.

The takeaway for defenders: Treat open-weight models like any other third-party code. Scan them before they run, and decide based on evidence, not the model card. Planting a backdoor now takes little more than a short fine-tuning run. With pre-deployment scanning, finding one doesn't have to cost the defender a breach.

This research is part of the CrowdStrike Cyber Superintelligence Lab's mission to build cyber defense that learns faster than adversaries evolve. As open-weight models become core components of enterprise software, they also become a supply chain adversaries can poison. Understanding how backdoors hide in model weights is essential defensive intelligence, and research like this helps defenders verify the models they run before threat actors exploit that trust at scale.

Title: Inside Falcon AI Gateway: One Control Point for AI Traffic
Context: Falcon AI Gateway, now generally available and included with CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian™, extends AI visibility and enforcement beyond the CrowdStrike Falcon® sensor
Full Text:
As AI agents move from answering questions to executing actions, seeing AI activity isn't enough. Security teams need to control it.

AI requests now come from employee assistants, coding agents, SaaS copilots, and custom applications and cloud workloads that call models directly through SDKs. Each of these requesters connects to model providers on its own, with its own credentials, models, and settings.

Falcon AI Gateway, now generally available and included with CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian™, extends AI visibility and enforcement beyond the CrowdStrike Falcon® sensor. It routes AI traffic through a centralized gateway to inspect prompts and responses, monitor usage, and enforce policy across managed and unmanaged devices.

One Control Point for Model Access, Usage, and Security

Discovery shows where unsanctioned AI is in use. Falcon AI Gateway adds a complementary approach: Make the approved path the only path.

Falcon AI Gateway authenticates each request, routes it to the right provider and model, applies usage limits, and applies Falcon Guardian policy both before the request reaches the provider and again when the response comes back.

Teams block direct connections to model providers using the network controls they already run, and route approved applications and workloads through Falcon AI Gateway. As a result, the AI traffic reaching providers from those workloads has passed through Falcon Guardian policy on the way. This doesn't discover or redirect AI traffic automatically; it gives teams a deliberate control point for the workloads they choose to route through it.

This allows teams to:

See: Traffic, models, tokens, and estimated spend in one place, with dashboards, request logs, and event data.

Adapt: Applications send requests to one gateway endpoint with one gateway key, using the API formats they already speak. Provider credentials stay in the gateway, and administrators can switch between connected model providers, such as Anthropic, Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, and Google Vertex AI, without reconfiguring every workload.

Control: Rate limits and budgets on requests, tokens, or estimated spend, scoped by application, user, team, model, or provider. Application keys suit services and shared workloads; personal keys attribute usage to an individual.

Secure: Falcon Guardian policy inspects prompts and responses routed through the gateway for risks such as prompt injection and sensitive data leakage.

Falcon AI Gateway and the Falcon sensor share one Falcon Guardian policy model, and each enforces where the policy sits. The sensor acts on the endpoint, including the local processes, files, and commands an agent runs. Falcon AI Gateway acts on traffic routed through it and can't stop local processes.

Because traffic flows through one point, AI Kill Switch in Falcon Guardian can cut off agents’ access to the model via the traffic routed through Falcon AI Gateway.

Falcon Guardian customers can find Falcon AI Gateway in the Falcon console under Falcon Experiences > AI Gateway. Developers connect an existing SDK or coding tool by changing the base URL to point at the gateway and using a gateway key.

Full Text:
CrowdStrike has been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape: Worldwide Augmented Identity Security Solutions 2026 Vendor Assessment.

Identity has become a critical attack surface. Adversaries exploit valid credentials to move laterally, escalate privileges, and operate undetected. Human, non-human, and AI agent identities continue to multiply across organizations, both expanding the attack surface and introducing new security challenges. AI agents in particular can autonomously access applications, invoke tools, and take action at machine speed, fundamentally changing how organizations must approach identity security.

Traditional identity security, built around static access decisions and periodic checks, can no longer keep pace. Organizations need continuous visibility into identity risk and the ability to enforce access decisions in real time.

We believe CrowdStrike's recognition as a Leader validates our approach to Continuous Identity, which brings together identity visibility, threat detection, privileged access, and real-time enforcement on the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform. With innovations like the recent CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider, we're extending our approach to secure AI agents with verifiable identities and tightly scoped, just-in-time access.

Identity Security for the Modern Enterprise

CrowdStrike capabilities demonstrate the value of Continuous Identity, from unified visibility and real-time risk intelligence to dynamic enforcement across the enterprise:

Unified endpoint and identity visibility: Identity attacks do not stay in one domain, and neither does our view of them. The CrowdStrike Falcon® sensor sees local and bypass authentication, network telemetry decrypts NTLM and SMB exchanges, and the identity graph updates in real time. By correlating endpoint and identity signals, CrowdStrike helps security teams identify suspicious behavior across the attack path and respond with greater context.

Rapid deployment: The Falcon platform brings identity and endpoint security together through one console and one sensor, which establishes identity visibility and coverage in hours to days. Policy templates, simulation, and audit modes support staged rollouts, which helps organizations operationalize identity security while minimizing disruption.

Real-time identity risk intelligence: CrowdStrike’s unified risk score updates in under a minute, includes blast radius, and feeds every downstream enforcement control with reevaluation after authentication and midsession intervention. These capabilities help security teams understand identity risk in context, prioritize threats, and make enforcement decisions. By connecting identity signals with security context from across the Falcon platform, CrowdStrike helps turn visibility into action.

Enforcement that keeps up with the session: CrowdStrike enforces zero standing privileges with auto-approved just-in-time elevation, bidirectional enforcement, post-authentication risk reevaluation, and mid-session intervention. This is Continuous Identity in practice: Access is continuously evaluated as risk changes, and privileges are adjusted or revoked when conditions warrant.

Standards participation: CrowdStrike leads working groups on CAEP, Shared Signals, RISC, and AuthZEN. These initiatives support interoperability and the exchange of identity risk signals across systems, helping organizations extend continuous identity security throughout their environments.

Together, these capabilities bring Continuous Identity to life, connecting visibility, risk intelligence, and real-time enforcement to help organizations stop identity-driven attacks.

CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider

CrowdStrike's approach to Continuous Identity goes beyond point-in-time authentication. By unifying identity posture management, threat detection, privileged access, and real-time enforcement on the Falcon platform, organizations can continuously assess identity risk, reduce standing privileges, and dynamically adjust or revoke access as risk changes.

As AI agents operate autonomously across enterprise environments, this approach is even more critical. CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider extends our Continuous Identity vision to AI agents with cryptographically verifiable identities, short-lived and tightly scoped access, and accountability by linking agent actions to the human or workload behind them.

The Future of Identity is Continuous

Identity security can no longer rely on point-in-time decisions. As human, non-human, and AI agent identities expand, organizations need continuous visibility into risk and the ability to enforce access in real time.

CrowdStrike is redefining identity security by moving beyond traditional approaches:

Static access becomes real-time control.

Fragmented tools become a unified platform.

Implicit trust becomes continuous, risk-based enforcement.

We believe CrowdStrike's recognition as a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape reinforces our vision for Continuous Identity and our commitment to securing every identity and stopping identity-driven attacks.

What is Augmented Identity Security?

Augmented Identity Security is an operating model that shifts identity management from static, periodic authentication to continuous, real-time risk evaluation. By fusing endpoint, directory, cloud, and runtime telemetry, augmented identity platforms continuously inspect session behavior, identify anomalous privilege escalation, and dynamically adjust or revoke access across human, machine, and AI agent identities.

Unlike legacy tools requiring dedicated domain controllers or network proxy infrastructure, Falcon Next-Gen Identity Security delivers immediate identity visibility and threat prevention through the existing single Falcon agent, which establishes coverage in hours to days.

CrowdStrike Agentic Identity Provider extends our Continuous Identity vision to AI agents with cryptographically verifiable identities, short-lived and tightly scoped access, and accountability by linking agent actions to the human or workload behind them.

Title: The XG Files: Falcon C2 Flying Under The (Browser) Radar
Context: They described it as a versatile tool for exploiting living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries (LOLBins)
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Unit 42 has identified Falcon (aka XG or Xiàng Gē), which is a command and control (C2) framework that compromises victims' browsers by running malicious JavaScript. An actor leveraged Falcon to compromise visitors of webmail portals and government web applications by placing malicious JavaScript directly within these sites.

Operating entirely inside the browser context, attackers have used the framework to sideload malicious Chrome extensions and steal the following information:

Passwords

Emails

Session cookies

Communications

Falcon also served as a delivery mechanism for an implant we call Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel.

Our analysis identified the compromise of government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. The campaigns we observed targeted ministries of foreign affairs, defense and interior, and law enforcement agencies, consistent with strategic intelligence collection objectives.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed in this article through the following products and services:

Advanced WildFire

Advanced URL Filtering and Advanced DNS Security

Cortex XDR and XSIAM

Cortex Agentic Endpoint Security

Prisma Browser

Idira Endpoint Privilege Manager (EPM)

Idira Identity and Access Management (IAM)

Organizations can access tailored adversary intelligence, direct analyst consultations, and specialized exposure tracking through Unit 42 Threat Intel Services and its Deep and Dark Web Service.

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

Related Unit 42 Topics

Command and Control (C2), Chrome. JavaScript

Hiding in Plain Sight

Falcon C2 management panels are designed to remain semi-hidden. When accessed, the panel displays a blank page with no visible branding or login interface.

To deter casual inspection, the page disables the right-click context menu via a global contextmenu listener that calls preventDefault(). The login form also stays hidden until the F9 key is pressed three consecutive times; any other keystroke resets the counter.

Figure 1 below shows the JavaScript code for this key tracking.

Once triggered, the page displays a branded Falcon panel featuring a stylized bird logo and credential input fields. This operational security (OPSEC) mechanism ensures that it does not directly expose the login page to bots, unintended visitors and automated systems that grab webpage screenshots.

Figure 2 below shows a screenshot of the login panel.

Falcon is written in NodeJS and has two listeners. One listener is for the management panel interface on TCP port 8080 and the victim-facing listener is on TCP port 443.

On the victim-facing listener, we observed a JavaScript-based version of the classic game Tetris serving as the default page, designed to blend in further. Another instance hosted a game of Snake. Figure 3 below shows both versions.

Overlap with PeckBirdy

In January 2026, Trend Micro reported on a scripting framework dubbed PeckBirdy. They described it as a versatile tool for exploiting living-off-the-land (LotL) binaries (LOLBins).

Our comparison with PeckBirdy revealed that it shares near-identical URL structures, payload delivery mechanisms and communication protocols with Falcon. Table 1 compares the URL structures of the two frameworks.

Table 1. URL structure comparison between Falcon and PeckBirdy.

Both frameworks use the same payload delivery sequence to execute HTA, HTML or JScript payloads, with the primary distinction being Falcon's inclusion of the /config/ path prefix.Both frameworks use AES for data encryption. PeckBirdy relies solely on AES with a predetermined encryption key, whereas Falcon negotiates an AES session key with the server, encrypted with RSA.Most significantly, both frameworks store their persistent session ID using the same Baidu-mimicking naming convention:

PeckBirdy writes its session ID to a browser cookie prefixed with Hm_lvt_

Falcon employs the same prefix for the same purpose, saving it as Hm_lvt_$ in the browser’s local storage and Hm_lvt__<session ID> within a browser cookie

Based on these extensive technical overlaps, we assess with high confidence that Falcon and PeckBirdy represent variants of the same core framework.

The Falcon Implant

When someone visits a website affected by Falcon, the website sends a request to the Falcon C2 server. The server generates an implant uniquely obfuscated for that browser session. The implant is generated by two files: victim_common.js and victim.js.

The first file holds the configuration block described below and the second file contains common functions for communication and command execution. The two files are combined, and then passed through an obfuscation routine that XOR encodes each character in the implant with a one-byte key and converts the result into an integer.

The result is a script with a large list of integers and a small section of code to decode and execute itself. Figure 4 shows an example of the obfuscated script.

Figure 5 shows the template configuration block. The $CLIENT_IP is the victim IP address, set by the server as it generates the implant.

Victim Persistence and Tracking

The implant generates a persistent 32-character lower case alphanumeric session identifier per victim using a three-tier storage strategy designed to survive session restarts:

Browser local storage: Reading and writing a key Hm_lvt_$, likely mimicking Baidu Analytics tracking identifiers to blend with legitimate Chinese web analytics telemetry

Cookie: Setting Hm_lvt__<session ID>=1 with a path of / and an expiry date of the year 2099

Falcon extension storage cache: Checking whether a storageApi object is defined; if so, the session ID is stored there as well

The storageApi is a dictionary within the Falcon browser extension, meaning it is present only if the victim has the Falcon browser extension installed. We detail the browser extension in the Falcon Browser Extension section.

C2 Communication

The implant establishes a TLS encrypted WebSocket connection to maintain a persistent connection as long as the browser tab of the affected webpage is open. It sends a heartbeat message {"heartbeat":"1"} every minute to keep the connection alive. The implant resets the timer on every inbound message, so an actively engaged session never emits standalone heartbeats.

The code supports a fallback protocol using the Comet communication protocol. If Comet is used, payload data exchanged with the C2 server is not encrypted. The WebSocket functionality supports AES encryption in combination with the TLS transport encryption as described below.

Cryptographic Key Exchange

The implant leverages the browser's native Web Crypto API to encrypt all exchanged data using AES. If the Web Crypto API is unavailable, the implant falls back to URL-encoding and Base64. The key exchange proceeds in five steps:

Step 1: The server offers its RSA public key

Upon WebSocket connection, the server pushes a message with an action pubkey containing a 2048-bit RSA public key in PEM format, as illustrated in Figure 6.

Step 2: The client generates 256-bit AES session key material

The implant generates a 32-byte AES key and a 16-byte initialization vector (IV) using the browser's crypto.getRandomValues. If unavailable, a fallback function generates the key material from an alphanumeric string.

Step 3: The client encrypts the session key material using the server’s RSA public key

Both the AES key and IV are individually encrypted using the server's RSA public key and then Base64-encoded.

Step 4: The client sends the encrypted AES key material to the server

The client sends the encrypted key material to the server in a key_exchange message, as shown in Figure 7.

Step 5: All subsequent exchanges have their payload data encrypted with the session key material using AES-256-CBC.

Command Dispatch

Following the key exchange, the implant registers with the server by sending information about its current execution environment. Figure 8 below shows the data before encryption.

The data includes the current URL and domain of the tab within which the Falcon implant is running. The data also includes the browser's User-Agent string and client IP address (set by the backend server during implant generation).

The implant first attempts to read the remark from the browser’s local storage, specifically from the _domain_google_mark field. If unsuccessful, it then searches for the string _domain_google_mark= within the current webpage’s cookies to retrieve the remark.

If the implant uses Comet for communication, it only supports the run and nothing commands, with the latter serving no operational purpose.

The run command enables an operator to execute arbitrary JavaScript code through evaluation by calling eval. The set_remark command applies a remark (or label/comment) to the session, helping the operator organize the sessions in the management panel. It updates the remark for the fields _domain_google_mark across the browser's local storage, document cookie and Falcon extension storage.

The implant implements four main command APIs that attackers can use in custom modules to exfiltrate data, notify an operator or annotate the session in the Falcon database. Table 2 below details the APIs.

Function

Purpose

xg_note

Set session label (remark)

xg_send

Send arbitrary JSON to the C2

xg_data

Exfiltrate arbitrary data

xg_notify

Send notification via Telegram

Table 2. Main command APIs.

Falcon Browser Extension

While the browser implant runs purely in the context of the browser tab, Falcon has two browser extensions to facilitate full control of a victim’s browser:

One for Firefox

One for Chrome

The extensions work with the implant.

We are currently unaware of how an operator is deploying these browser extensions. It is likely that they are using an initial implant to trick a target into installing the browser extension and granting the operator unfettered browser access.

The two extensions are functionally identical, this section focuses on the Chrome extension.

The extension masquerades as a PDF reader, as shown in Figure 9, using the name PDF Viewer.

The extension consists of 14 files, as detailed below in Table 3.

An operator generates the extension bundle in the management panel, which provides the operator a ZIP archive that is ready to install in a victim’s browser. As manually installing an extension in Chrome involves many steps, it is possible that an operator instead socially engineered a victim into downloading and executing a small deployment utility that installed the extension via the command line.

We have observed evidence in the management panel that the operator possesses a utility for silent plugin installation for Chrome and Firefox as Figure 10 below shows. However, we have not been able to recover a sample for further analysis.

The operator can upload tools to the management panel and password protect them, preventing other people from accessing them. The panel shows that there are two tools uploaded. Table 4 below shows the translated columns.

The extension requests a total of 40 permissions that grant the operator full control over the victim’s browser. These permissions include access to credentials, cookies and browser network traffic. Figure 11 below shows the extension manifest.

The manifest parameters are described below in Table 5.

Extension Initialization

When the extension is installed, enabled, or the browser starts, Chrome parses the extension manifest. The background service worker, background.js, runs and creates a hidden or offscreen document from the offscreen.html file.

The offscreen.html file loads offscreen.js (hereafter referred to as offscreen) and creates an iframe to load sandbox.html (which loads sandbox.js, hereafter referred to as sandbox) in parallel.

This structure is common for Chrome extensions that need offscreen documents. The sandbox acts as a code execution environment, allowing eval execution.

Offscreen starts by creating a MessageChannel message bus for communication

between extension components. It delays execution for 2 seconds to allow the message bus to be established before sending a request to the C2 server to download the Falcon implant. The code is passed to the sandbox through the message bus as shown in Figure 12.

The code is executed by appending a script tag to the sandbox.html document body. The implant code, now running inside the sandbox, establishes a WebSocket connection to the C2 server.

In parallel with the background/offscreen initialization, Chrome automatically injects content-script.js (hereafter referred to as content script) into every page visited by the victim due to its manifest definition in content_scripts.

The twitter-dm.js script is injected only if a victim visits twitter[.]com or x[.]com as defined in the manifest. The content script runs in an isolated context and only has access to the webpage's Document Object Model (DOM), but not to its JavaScript context.

To achieve full page context access, the content script injects a script tag into the page pointing to chrome-extension://<extension ID>/analytics-core.js (hereafter called analytics core). Because the analytics core file is defined in web_accessible_resources in the manifest, it is accessible to web pages and not blocked by CORS.

At this point, the extension has:

Full access to the browser's data store (via chrome.* APIs in background.js)

Full access to the context of every webpage the victim visits (via the content script and analytics core)

Web Proxy

Falcon allows an operator to use a victim’s browser as a proxy server and to use the victim’s browser data store, including session cookies and credentials for requests. An operator creates a proxy and attaches it to the victim’s Falcon session.

The operator then configures the victim’s browser with the Falcon server address and the designated proxy port. The operator is then able to send requests to the Falcon implant within the victim’s browser, with these requests encapsulated in a JavaScript snippet. They will then be sent to the victim’s browser as illustrated below in Figure 13.

The sandbox receives and executes the JavaScript. This script calls handleProxyRequest with the request data as an argument, which subsequently sends a message on the Chrome runtime message bus as shown in Figure 14.

The background service worker picks up the messages, constructs the request and sets the fetchOptions to use the victim's credential store in the request. Figure 15 below shows this, highlighted in bold.

The response from the request is Base64-encoded and returned in JSON via the C2 WebSocket. This enables an operator to browse resources using the identity of the victim, allowing for session hijacking and access to internal network resources.

Download Intercept

The extension can intercept and replace file downloads according to operator-defined rules. The operator can define broad rules targeting a list of domain and file extensions.

Figure 16 below shows an example rule that intercepts and replaces all executable downloads from google[.]com and dl.google[.]com with an operator-controlled URL.

The background service worker installs an event listener that listens for chrome.downloads.onCreated events. When detected, the background worker sends a message to offscreen over the Chrome runtime message bus, which it relays to the sandbox.

The sandbox applies the intercept rule set to the download URL to determine whether it should modify the URL. While the background service worker has the necessary privileges to intercept and replace downloads, the extension's architectural design keeps the intercept rules and C2 command processing (which requires eval execution) within the sandbox. This design necessitates passing messages across the message buses.

If the URL matches a rule, the extension cancels the original file transfer and removes the download from the Chrome download history. The new URL consists of the target and redirect URL, where the target URL is encoded and appended to the end of the redirect URL as shown below in Figure 17.

The download retains the original filename and will appear to the victim as ChromeSetup.exe while the origins will show as evil[.]com.

This technique enables an operator to achieve code execution on the victim’s system by intercepting a legitimate download and replacing it with the operator’s payload. It does so leaving little evidence that the file originated from a malicious source. The operator can use this to deploy additional malware and gain a stronger foothold in the target network.

Network Hooking

The functionality of analytics core is to install a hook for window.fetch, XMLHttpRequest.open and XMLHttpRequest.send. This hook enables the extension to intercept requests made from the current webpage and any third-party scripts loaded on the page. The operator can also define intercept rules that can replace a URL with an operator’s own URL (e.g., to hijack software updates).

For window.fetch, the hook intercepts HTTP requests that result in an HTTP 200 response and sets the content type to application/json or contains text/. The intercepted request and response data is posted to the MessageChannel as shown below in Figure 18.

For calls to XMLHttpRequest.send, the hook checks whether the HTTP response code is between 200 and 299, and whether the content type is application/json or contains text/. The hook also checks the responseType attribute to see whether it is text or an empty string.

The intercepted request and response data is posted to the MessageChannel as shown below in Figure 19.

The posted message signals the content script to relay the message from the MessageChannel onto Chrome’s runtime message bus using chrome.runtime.sendMessage as shown below in Figure 20.

The background worker picks up the message and stores it in a cache awaiting operator instructions to upload the data to the C2 server. The cache operates in a FIFO fashion and stores a maximum of 500 requests.

Discord Messages and Friends List Exfiltration

An operator can also target Discord chat messages and friend lists. They achieve this using passive network hooking described above, as Discord uses JSON in its HTTP communication. If configured, the operator can intercept requests matching a Discord URL pattern with victim data stored in a separate table.

Zalo Chat Database Exfiltration

Zalo is a chat application similar to WhatsApp that is popular in Vietnam. Falcon supports intercepting Zalo chat message databases using passive network hooking. Targeting Zalo provides additional insights into the targeted audience of the operator.

Gmail Exfiltration

While the ability to exfiltrate Gmail data is not a core functionality of the extension, it does provide an operator with the access needed to compromise a victim’s Gmail account and download email data. An operator issues a command that uploads a JavaScript to the extension, which sends a request to Gmail using the user’s Gmail session cookie to retrieve a list of authenticated users.

An operator can then select the accounts to collect data from, to be uploaded to the C2 server. This action is facilitated by the extension.

Clipboard Hijacking

As soon as the extension is installed, loaded or the browser starts, the clipboard hijacker is actively monitoring the victim’s clipboard events. It intercepts every cut, copy and paste event by adding document listeners as shown below in Figure 21.

By default, the hijacker runs without any rules. An operator has the option to define pattern matching rules and replacements (e.g., replacing account numbers or cryptocurrency wallet addresses).

The rules are stored in Chrome’s local storage chrome.storage.local in a key clipboard_replacer_rules. Figure 22 below shows an example rule.

Intercepted clipboard events are passed as messages on Chrome’s message bus. These messages are picked up by the background worker and stored in a cache similar to the intercepted HTTP requests. They then await an operator command to upload the data.

X/Twitter Direct Messages Exfiltration

The extension comes with a separate module for scraping direct messages from the X/Twitter social media platform. The module is defined in the extension manifest under content_scripts and is injected into any webpage whose URL matches the patterns *://*.twitter.com/* or *://*.x.com/*.

The module can only scrape direct messages when a victim browses a conversation. It cannot enumerate conversations or open other conversations.

Possible AI-Assisted Development

The Falcon framework shows a high level of complexity in both design and capability. However, the overall code exhibits characteristics suggesting the malware authors likely used AI to assist with design and development. This conclusion is based on the coding style, including variable naming and code comments.

There are also inconsistent design choices that make little sense to a human developer. For example, the network hook for XMLHttpRequest checks for an HTTP response code greater than or equal to 200 but less than 300, while the hook for fetch checks against response.ok. Both result in the same outcome while the first is rarely, if ever, used when the response.ok shortcut exists.

In Southeast Asian country A, the operator used Falcon to load a custom username-harvesting module. This was followed later by a fake Adobe Flash update prompt that attempted to deliver the Antino implant to pre-selected users.

Middle Eastern Country (Roundcube Webmail)

In April 2026, we observed a Falcon implant residing on the Roundcube webmail portal of a Middle Eastern Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The actor had injected a <script> tag into the portal header as shown in Figure 23.

The resource config_r5lfmqe3 returns the obfuscated JavaScript Falcon implant. This enables the actor to intercept credentials as users sign in. Based on the analyzed data, we assess with high confidence that the script executes on each Roundcube visited by a victim, granting the operator access to a victim’s inbox and account settings.

We observed a total of 39 Roundcube instances being affected within the target country. We have no evidence of any instances affected outside of the target country, suggesting this was a highly targeted campaign.

Title: CERT-In’s CRAFTY FALCON Advisory: AI Is the Accelerant, Your Payment APIs Are the Target
Context: CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling...
Full Text:
CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling its victims' own payment and disbursement APIs. Organizations that fixed their systems after CERT-In's first warning in October have been hit again.

The AI label will get the headlines. The attack chain tells a plainer story. Hardcoded API tokens, staging servers that share credentials with production, IP allow-lists that trust shared third-party fetchers: none of these weaknesses is new. What the AI tooling changes is the time between an attacker finding one and cashing it out, and that time is now shorter than most remediation cycles.

What CERT-In has confirmed

The latest advisory updates the previous Oct. 9 advisory. CERT-In's finance team, CSIRT-Fin, named the actor and called the campaign active and ongoing, with victims across NBFCs, digital lenders, fintechs, payment aggregators, payment service providers and crypto exchanges.

Entities that had received the earlier restricted advisories and remediated were deliberately hit again, some after incomplete cleanup, with attacks timed for holidays and weekends.

CERT-In names four publicly available offensive AI tools: ARTEX, the PentAGI multi-agent pentest system, the Cairn attack search engine and CyberStrikeAI. It doesn't attribute the actor or say how many entities were hit. Business Standard reported that researchers link at least two of the tools to China, but where a tool was written says little about who ran it.

How CRAFTY FALCON gets from a staging server to a mule account

The advisories describe four stages:

Get in. Exposed UAT and staging servers, file-upload and deserialization flaws exploited as soon as they're public, hardcoded API tokens, forged repository commits, plaintext credentials and services without MFA.

Reach production. Credentials and network paths shared with production carry the attacker across. AWS Systems Manager and Lambda then run commands through legitimate cloud channels.

Get past the app. The attacker reverse-engineers the app, calls APIs from a modified package and routes traffic through allow-listed third-party fetcher IPs that anyone can make fetch a URL.

Test, cash out, clean up. A Rs 1 transfer confirms the route. Large transfers follow to mule accounts at several banks, including through merchant settlement APIs, and crypto platforms lose wallet keys. Logs and endpoint tools get tampered with.

Because the calls come from the victim's own allow-listed infrastructure, the October advisory says they bypass KYC, beneficiary verification, balance and per-transaction limit checks. To the payment partner, the fraud looks like normal traffic.

Also read: Addressing Deepfake Risks in BFSI: Why Early Detection Is Critical

The real story: AI took away the grace period

Is "AI-driven" doing too much work here? Partly. Hardcoded tokens, plaintext credentials and missing MFA were in the October advisory before the AI tools took center stage.

What the tooling changes is cost and tempo. CERT-In says the frameworks run full attack chains on their own, refine tailored scripts in rapid succession, adapt payloads to how the target responds and rotate infrastructure within hours. Reverse-engineering one lender's app used to be a project. Now an agent can work through a target list.

That explains the re-targeting. An agent can come back, test whether the fix was complete and try the next path on a Saturday night. Patching in the next sprint assumes an attacker who gets tired. This one doesn't.

Who's exposed

Any Indian entity that can move money through an API: lenders with disbursement APIs, aggregators with settlement APIs, fintechs holding partner-bank credentials and crypto exchanges with hot wallets. You're most exposed if an internet-facing non-production environment shares anything with production, or if your payment API trusts the client app or a source IP instead of a signed, server-validated request.

What to do this week

CERT-In lists 27 actions. Start with the six that break the money path:

Cut non-production off from production. No shared credentials, keys, databases or routes, and alert on any UAT-to-production access.

Stop trusting the client and the source IP. Validate server-side, sign requests with a nonce and timestamp, use app attestation, and swap fetcher IP allow-lists for mutual TLS or scoped keys.

Retire long-lived secrets. Scan repositories and CI/CD for secrets, move to short-lived scoped tokens and rotate build and deployment tokens now.

Hold the Rs 1 pattern. Flag micro-value transfers to new beneficiaries followed by large ones, and add cooling periods and maker-checker approval on merchant settlements.

Watch the cloud control plane. Alert in AWS CloudTrail on Systems Manager sessions and SendCommand, Lambda UpdateFunctionCode in production and new IAM users, roles or keys. Default-deny server egress.

Staff the weekend and assume persistence. Lower holiday alert thresholds and verify eradication forensically.

What we're watching

The offensive tools are compromised too, though nothing ties this to CRAFTY FALCON. Researcher Badbyte recently said that a GitHub copy of ARTEX pulled a Docker image with a hidden root shell, and 62 internet-facing consoles served it between Nov. 2 and 4. It's one more reason CERT-In wants these tools banned from corporate infrastructure.

November 2026 Attack Surface Analysis

Preview-pane-triggered exploitation remains a dominant attack surface pattern for the third consecutive month, with eight Critical RCE vulnerabilities across Microsoft Office applications including Outlook and Word. CVE-2026-110043 and CVE-2026-110068 in Outlook exemplify the risk: Merely selecting a malicious message in the Reading Pane or previewing an attachment in File Explorer triggers code execution without any click or macro prompt. This attack pattern continues to be attractive to phishing operators and initial access brokers because it converts document or message delivery into reliable code execution, bypassing the user-action barrier that many enterprises treat as a training backstop.

Identity platform components face elevated risk this month with Critical flaws in both Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) and Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS). CVE-2026-119958 enables RCE against LDAP, while CVE-2026-118146 and CVE-2026-118148 target AD DS with RCE and elevation-of-privilege attack paths, respectively. These protocols underpin domain authentication and authorization for every joined workstation and server; successful exploitation of either can cascade to domain-wide compromise. Similar identity fabric vulnerabilities have historically been targeted by advanced adversaries seeking persistent access to enterprise environments.

Windows Hyper-V sees an unusually high concentration of privilege escalation vulnerabilities this month, with eight CVEs spanning multiple flaw classes. CVE-2026-113753, CVE-2026-113856, and CVE-2026-113860 all enable elevation of privilege within the hypervisor boundary. Hyper-V underpins Azure compute infrastructure and endpoint features such as Windows Sandbox, Credential Guard, and other Virtualization-Based Security capabilities, so the exposure extends beyond dedicated virtualization hosts to ordinary Windows endpoints with these features enabled.

Legacy network services including Server Message Block (SMB) and Print Spooler continue to draw Critical-severity RCE findings, reinforcing the persistent risk these widely deployed components carry. The unauthenticated network-reachable RCE cluster spans 14 CVEs this month, with Windows Message Queuing (MSMQ) vulnerabilities such as CVE-2026-109459 and CVE-2026-116710 representing exposure on any system with MSMQ enabled. These services listen on the network by design and often lack authentication requirements for initial protocol negotiation, making any exposed instance an immediate target for opportunistic scanning. This class of legacy network service has historically been targeted in wormable exploitation scenarios.

Exploited Zero-Day Spoofing Vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook

CVE-2026-124194 is a Moderate spoofing vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook with a CVSS score of 6.5, and Microsoft confirms it is being exploited in the wild. The flaw stems from the product UI failing to warn users of unsafe actions: A specially crafted message file can cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the usual external-content warning, disclosing the victim's NTLMv2 hash.

Outlook is the default mail client across most enterprise Windows deployments, making any flaw that bypasses user safety prompts a direct initial access vector at scale. Exploitation requires the victim to open a malicious file delivered via email or another channel. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector for this particular CVE. Once the victim opens the file, Outlook silently initiates an outbound connection, and the captured NTLMv2 hash can be relayed or cracked offline to impersonate the user against other services that accept NTLM authentication.

The Moderate severity rating reflects the user interaction requirement, but the real-world exposure is broader than the score suggests. Credential disclosure flaws that require only a file open, bypass visible warnings, and yield reusable authentication material are a well-established technique in targeted intrusion campaigns. Similar spoofing primitives in Outlook have historically drawn attention from both commodity phishing operators and advanced adversaries seeking footholds in enterprise environments.

Critical RCE Vulnerabilities in Windows Services

CVE-2026-112967 and CVE-2026-116928 are Critical RCE vulnerabilities in Windows services, each carrying a CVSS score of 9.8. Both allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code over the network, though they affect distinct components with different deployment realities.

CVE-2026-112967 is a heap-based buffer overflow in the Windows Xbox Live Networking Service. An in-network attacker can call arbitrary endpoints on the service to trigger the flaw. Enterprise exposure depends on whether the service is present and running. Consumer-oriented Windows SKUs and gaming-enabled configurations are the primary population, making this lower priority for most corporate fleets.

CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in the Windows Search component. The attack path is notable: An unauthenticated attacker can send an email with a specially crafted attachment to an Exchange Server, and the search indexer processes the attachment automatically for indexing. The recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Successful exploitation grants code execution with the permissions of the indexing service. Windows Search is broadly deployed and tightly integrated with Exchange for mailbox indexing, which places this flaw on an email delivery attack surface that reaches internet-facing mail infrastructure. The Windows Search path is the more significant exposure for enterprise environments. Email-delivered payloads that trigger without user interaction have historically been attractive to targeted intrusion operators because they bypass the phishing-click dependency that slows most initial access campaigns.
